deep.reconstruction:
This page is a working draft of §§10–11 of Riemann's Göttingen doctoral dissertation (1851), 'Grundlagen für eine allgemeine Theorie der Functionen einer veränderlichen complexen Grösse'. The previous page has the definition of a winding point (Windungspunkt) and a draft petition to the faculty for admission to the disputation, which fits this dating. The next page drafts the regularity theorem built on log r.

(1) Additivity of the Green boundary integral.
- Setting: a surface T_1 is split into two pieces T_2 and T_3. Let u, u' be functions on T, p the normal direction to the boundary and ds the arc length.
- Claim: the boundary integral ∫(u ∂u'/∂p − u' ∂u/∂p) ds over ∂T_3 equals the integral over ∂T_1 minus the integral over ∂T_2.
- Implicit reason (mine): by Green's second identity each boundary integral equals ±∬(u Δu' − u' Δu) dT over the corresponding piece, and area integrals are additive. Equivalently, along the common cut the normals of T_2 and T_3 point in opposite directions, so the two contributions cancel.
- Riemann waves the rest through with 'u.s.w.'; the point is that the formula can be applied piece by piece, which licenses cutting out small discs around singular points.

(2) Theorem I, maximum principle (several formulations struck out).
- The surviving sense: u, satisfying the hypotheses of the preceding § (harmonic, Δu = 0, inside T), cannot have a value at an interior point O that is greater, or smaller, than at all surrounding points.
- The argument uses the mean-value theorem proved in the preceding §: u_0 = (1/2π) ∫_0^{2π} u dφ over any circle centred at O, i.e. ∫_0^{2π} (u − u_0) dφ = 0.
- This equation could not hold if u − u_0 had the same sign everywhere in such a disc around O. Hence there is no strict interior extremum.

(3) Transition and Theorem II.
- Transition: 'Under the same hypotheses, from the conclusion of §1 the following theorems therefore result.'
- Theorem II: u cannot have a constant value in one part of T and a different value in another part. In modern terms this is the identity theorem / unique continuation for harmonic functions on a connected surface.
- The proof begins, 'If u had everywhere the value … in a part A of the surface T …', and breaks off. It presumably continues on the next sheet in the published form, where the mean-value property is applied at points on the boundary of A.
errors: No mathematical error on the page. The mean-value argument as stated excludes only a strict extremum, i.e. u − u_0 of strict one sign on a whole disc. The non-strict case (u ≤ u_0 with equality somewhere) needs an extra continuity step that is not written here: a vanishing integral of a nonpositive continuous function forces u ≡ u_0 on the circle.

The proof of Theorem II is only begun. In the published dissertation the corresponding argument (sign of u − a next to the region where u = a) is known to be sketchy, because u − a need not have one sign near the boundary of A. A rigorous proof uses real-analyticity, or the connectedness of the set where u is locally constant.

The sign bookkeeping in the additivity statement depends on the orientation convention for p (Riemann uses the inward normal). The difference formula ∂T_3 = ∂T_1 − ∂T_2 is correct only when the normals are oriented consistently relative to each piece.

results.what: Additivity of the boundary integral ∫(u u'_p − u' u_p) ds under decomposition of the surface
results.modern_name: Green's second identity / additivity over subdomains (cancellation along cuts)

results.what: Mean value property ∫_0^{2π} (u − u_0) dφ = 0 for harmonic u, used as a tool
results.modern_name: Gauss mean value theorem for harmonic functions

results.what: A harmonic function has no strict interior maximum or minimum
A harmonic function constant on a subregion is constant everywhere
results.modern_name: Identity theorem / unique continuation for harmonic functions
